query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the Co‐free FeNiCrMn high‐entropy alloy, the dynamic mechanical response is primarily controlled by grain-boundary–mediated heterogeneous nucleation of 1/6⟨112⟩ partial dislocations leading to stacking fault formation. The removal of Co reduces the stacking fault energy compared to the traditional equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, thereby lowering the nucleation barrier at specific grain boundaries. Under high strain rates and low temperatures, this mechanism dominates and causes an earlier onset of stress drops and increased stacking fault density; at elevated temperatures, increased thermal activation promotes dynamic recovery, moderating these effects.
generation.material_initial_state: As-solidified, single-phase solid solution of Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy with a polycrystalline (or bicrystal) microstructure including well-characterized grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Perform controlled tensile deformation experiments (or corresponding high-rate simulations) on bicrystal or polycrystalline samples with defined GB character (for example, comparing Σ3 versus Σ9 or Σ19 boundaries) under varying temperatures and strain rates.
generation.conditions: Tensile testing at temperatures ranging from room temperature (~300 K) to elevated temperatures (~1000 K) and strain rates between 10^7 and 10^9 s⁻¹; all tests conducted on samples prepared in the as-solidified, single-phase state.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary structures (e.g., Σ3, Σ9, Σ19) that serve as preferential sites for nucleating partial dislocations and the subsequent formation of stacking faults.
generation.mechanism: The reduced stacking fault energy from omitting Co enhances the ease with which grain boundaries nucleate 1/6⟨112⟩ partial dislocations. At lower temperatures and/or higher strain rates, this results in earlier dislocation nucleation and rapid stacking fault formation, which in turn impedes further dislocation motion and raises the strain-hardening rate. At higher temperatures, thermally activated processes facilitate dynamic recovery, offsetting the early nucleation effects and resulting in a softened response.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline (either equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi or single crystal samples), Co-free samples will exhibit: (a) a lower critical strain for the onset of dislocation nucleation (evidenced by a stress drop in the stress–strain curve), (b) a higher density of stacking faults at the onset of plasticity (especially in GB regions with higher nucleation efficiency), and (c) a transition from a pronounced stress-drop behavior at low temperatures/high strain rates to smoother flow at elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the behavior of either equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy or single crystals where grain-boundary effects are absent, under comparable deformation conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to as-solidified, single-phase HEAs deformed in tension (or corresponding high-rate deformation modes) and is most relevant in regimes where grain boundary nucleation is the dominant source of dislocation activity. It may not hold if secondary phases or significant microstructural inhomogeneities are present.
generation.uncertainty: The exact reduction in nucleation strain and the magnitude of the stress drop (and stacking fault density differences) are uncertain due to potential variations in local grain boundary chemistry and structure, as well as the interplay with thermally activated recovery processes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of bicrystal (or well-textured polycrystalline) samples of the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy with controlled and characterized grain boundary types (e.g., Σ3 vs Σ9). Perform tensile tests across a range of temperatures (300 K to 1000 K) and strain rates (10^7 to 10^9 s⁻¹). In parallel, conduct the same experiments on a Co-containing (equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi) alloy and on single crystals (lacking GB influence) as baselines.
measurements: Record stress–strain curves to identify the onset of stress drops (indicative of dislocation nucleation).
Characterize the density and spatial distribution of stacking faults and partial dislocations (using in situ microscopy or post-mortem transmission electron microscopy).
Quantify differences in nucleation strain and ultimate strength across different GB types and test conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Co-free samples do not exhibit a systematically lower nucleation strain and higher initial stacking fault density at low temperatures/high strain rates relative to the baseline, or if the temperature dependence of the stress–strain response does not show the predicted transition (i.e., absence of a clear shift from sharp stress drops to smoother flow at elevated temperatures), then the hypothesis that GB-mediated partial dislocation nucleation (modulated by reduced stacking fault energy due to Co removal) governs the dynamic behavior is falsified.

While the Cantor alloy has been the subject of numerous studies in recent years, most of these have been mainly focused on the effects of element compositions away from the equiatomic one, stacking fault energies,, and lattice distortions. The role of GBs in the mechanical deformation of HEA alloys remains poorly understood. Tensile stress-strain diagrams for Cantor alloy bicrystals with [110] and [111] loading axes show that GBs facilitate the nucleation of partial dislocations, which with further deformation grow in the bulk crystal leaving behind stacking faults. This is in agreement with recent experimental findings demonstrating that GBs act as nucleation sites for mechanical nanotwins,. The bicrystals with a [111] loading axis were found to require more mechanical energy to nucleate dislocations from GBs compared to systems with a [110] loading axis. As shown in Figs. 5 and 6, nucleation of 1/6⟨112⟩ dislocations in the bicrystal systems occurred at lower strain values compared to their single crystal counterparts.
